title: Affective Design Analysis of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): A User-Centric Perspective
tldr: Affective trust calibration is a viable route for XAI alongside cognitive processing, with explanation form, communication style, and supplementary information being the key design components users seek in effective XAI.
problem_and_motivation: Current XAI research predominantly focuses on developer needs rather than end-user requirements, limiting adoption. Most XAI techniques require ML/DL expertise that typical end-users lack, and existing approaches treat explanations purely as cognitive resources rather than as design elements that influence user emotions and trust.
approach: Conducted a pre-study with 312 AI users to identify familiar AI systems and design attributes users consider important for XAI.
Designed a between-subject experiment testing 64 design configurations (2^6) with 3 design attributes and AI features across 202 qualified participants.
Developed a Figma-based experimental testbed simulating image classification AI with Google Lens as template, testing participants over two days.
Used Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with covariance-based optimization for causal relationship analysis via two-stage methodology.
Applied Exploratory Factor Analysis and Confirmatory Factor Analysis to validate measurement instruments.
findings: num: 12 of 21 hypothesized direct relationships were statistically supported.
num: 202 participants from initial 234 qualified after screening.
Affective route confirmed as viable trust calibration path alongside cognitive route for XAI.
Example-based explanation form increased interestingly surprised and trusting emotions and perceived usefulness.
Logic-robotic communication style increased fearfully dismayed and anxiously suspicious emotions and decreased perceived usefulness.
num: 4 moderators identified as significant: AI anxiety (p=0.005), incidental emotion (p<0.001), AI reliability (p<0.001), and experience (p=0.036).
key_figures_tables: Figure 1: XAI Trust Calibration Model -> Proposes affective and cognitive routes as parallel trust calibration paths in XAI.
Table 8: Mediation effect analysis -> Interestingly surprised, trusting, and fearfully dismayed emotions significantly mediated trust and reliance paths.
Table 10: Global moderation effect analysis -> AI anxiety, incidental emotion, reliability, and experience identified as significant moderators.

definitions.definition: Explainable Artificial Intelligence - techniques that provide human-level explanations of AI decision-making processes.
The dynamic process of adjusting trust levels toward an AI system based on performance, reliability, and interaction experience.
Trust formation path based on emotional responses to stimuli rather than rational or cognitive evaluation.
Trust formation path based on rational evaluation of a system's behavior, performance, and capabilities.
Structural Equation Modeling - a statistical method for testing causal relationships between latent variables.
XAI Emotion Set - a validated emotion classification framework for measuring user emotional responses to XAI.
Elaboration Likelihood Model - a theory describing central vs peripheral processing in persuasion and attitude change.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper is the first to empirically verify that affective processing serves as a viable trust calibration route for XAI, complementing the previously dominant cognitive route.
directly_justifies: Affective processing is a viable trust calibration route for XAI alongside cognitive processing.
Example-based explanation form increases positive emotions and perceived usefulness in XAI.
Logic-robotic communication style increases negative emotions and decreases perceived usefulness.
AI anxiety, incidental emotion, AI reliability, and experience significantly moderate trust calibration.
limits: Study limited to visual imagery XAI type in image recognition context, may not generalize to other XAI forms.
Two-day experience window may not capture long-term trust dynamics.
Single domain (image classification) limits cross-domain generalizability.
